_bootstrapToleranceNote: The bar a configuration must clear to mint its FIRST self-baseline. A new configuration has no prior to check against, so the only available question is whether its numbers are plausible at all — and the oracle is the only reference. This is deliberately NOT the parity bar: parity asks whether the editions agree and is now tight enough (2e-04 Hz / 1e-04 dB) that a new port still being built could fail it, which would leave that port with no zero-tolerance regression check at exactly the moment it most needs one. Failing parity is a finding to investigate; failing this means the numbers are garbage and must not be frozen.
_gatedFftSignal: Synthetic, 48000 Hz, 0.4 s; computeGatedFFT; dB at the bin nearest the target. Kept top-level rather than inside gatedFft: consumers decode gatedFft as a map of case objects, and a sibling string there breaks a typed decoder.
_generator: GENERATED by the Swift GenerateParityOracle test target, via Tooling/mint-oracle.sh in the GuitarTap repo — never by hand. Only Swift mints: a tracking edition minting would make the oracle record what the tracking edition does, which is precisely backwards. The generator seeds from this file and rewrites only filePlayback, gatedFft, oracleVersion, generatedAt and configuration; every other key here, including these notes, is hand-maintained and survives a mint untouched — which is why this one has to be kept honest by hand. Process, including the publish-before-you-sync rule and what to do with the re-mint diff: guitar-tap-project/tooling/parity/README.md. Values are measurements: change them by minting and reviewing the diff, never by editing this file.
_selfToleranceNote: Three bars, three questions. tolerances is CROSS-EDITION parity: do the editions agree? Measured 2026-10-19 on nine configurations — Swift on macOS, on iPad and iPhone devices and on the iOS simulator; Python and the web on macOS, Linux and Windows — the worst distances from this oracle are 2.04e-05 Hz, 1.16e-05 dB, 4.17e-06 dB in the gated FFT, 6.67e-07 in q and 1.51e-09 s in ring-out. All of it is Swift's float32 vDSP chain against Python's and the web's float64: Python and the web agree to about 1e-14, one operating system against another not at all, and an iOS device computes exactly what macOS does (the simulator differs from both in the last bit of a few values). So the bars sit at about ten times the worst: 2e-04 Hz, 1e-04 dB, 5e-05 dB, 1e-05 and 2e-08 s — loose enough for a new runtime's last bit, tight enough that a real divergence cannot hide beneath them. selfTolerances is SAME-EDITION, SAME-CONFIGURATION: did this configuration change? Nothing legitimately moves it, so it is 1e-12 rather than zero only because one configuration (OS × arch) runs on different CPUs — GitHub's runners, different people's machines — whose vectorised maths can differ in the last bit (7e-15 seen between Linux runners, 2026-10-10); 1e-12 covers that and is still a million times below the smallest real change (~1e-6). bootstrapTolerances gates a new configuration's first mint. One number cannot do these jobs — the old shared 1 dB figure hid sub-0.003 dB drift in the Swift goldens for an unknown length of time.
_toleranceProvenanceNote: tolerances measures the state of 2026-10-19, after every edition began aligning the guitar capture window to the tap's onset as Swift does — which shrank the cross-edition spread about 400-fold from the 0.0076 Hz / 0.0030 dB the bars were first set from. Do not read these numbers as permanent: a later change that brings the editions closer (or a new edition) is the signal to re-measure with tooling/parity-report.py and tighten again; a sudden jump in the headroom it reports is the expected consequence of such a change, not an anomaly. Why frequency moves more than dB: peak frequency comes from a parabola through three dB bins, and guitar back modes are broad (curvature -0.4 dB against air's -4.4), so the fit reaches -2.455 bins/dB and a dB difference becomes about 1.8 times as many Hz (2.455 bins/dB x 0.7324 Hz/bin). freqHz is not an independent measurement — the 1e-04 dB bar gives 1.8e-04 Hz, which is why the frequency bar is 2e-04. Tighten the two together or not at all.

REG-B2._note: Brace at numberOfTaps=3 — the brace counterpart to REG-P2: REG-P2 is PLATE multi-tap and REG-B1 single-tap brace, so this is the case that exercises brace averaging. Deliberately a harder case than the other material fixtures: the UMIK-1 is on its 18 dB gain path, so the peak sits at -65.5 dB against a -63.9 dB detection threshold. The peak is read off the AVERAGED spectrum, not the last tap.

REG-G1._ringOutNote: The tap's ring-out, measured from its FFT window: the level over a sliding 1024-sample window from the onset, peak to 15 dB below it, interpolated between samples. It does not depend on where the chunk boundaries fall, so the editions agree to rounding.

REG-G2._perTapNote: Taps 1 and 7 select 296.5 Hz as Back rather than ~240.6 Hz. That is the real behaviour of the shared peak-selection path on this fixture, not a transcription slip - it is pinned deliberately so a change in selection shows up.

REG-P2._note: 3 taps PER PHASE (9 total), recorded by the web app. Each phase averages, and the peak is read off the AVERAGED spectrum - not the last tap, which is the bug this case pins. A regression to last-tap selection is what this case catches: the masked deltas were fL 0.94, fC 0.81, fLC 2.62 dB.
